sentences.text: Her father had seen the seal and would not discuss it.
This was unusual, because her father discussed everything.
He was a man who could take twenty minutes to explain a decision about diesel.

But if the seal came up — and it came up, because it came up in that bay the way the weather comes up — he would go quiet and busy, and find something that needed doing with his hands, and the conversation would move on without him.
Maeve worked out the year from other people.
It had been the year before she was born.

The boat he had then had gone on the rocks at the north end in a February gale, with nobody aboard, because he had not gone out that morning, and the not going out was the part nobody explained properly.
He had lost the boat and the gear and, for nine months, the licence.
She asked her grandmother about it once, in the kitchen, when they were podding peas.
Her grandmother did not look up.
"He'd made his mind up," she said.
"To do what?" "To go to Liverpool.
He had a cousin there and a job at the end of it.

He'd told me and he'd told your mother and he'd gone down to the pier that evening to look at the water and say goodbye to it, which is a thing men here do and pretend they don't." She pushed a pod open with her thumb.
"He was twenty-four and he'd been on the water since he was younger than you and there was nothing left in this bay for him.
That's not a mood, love.
That's a sum.
He did the sum and the sum came out Liverpool." She was quiet for a moment.
Peas went into the bowl.
"I'd have gone with him.
I want you to know that, because you'll hear it told differently by people who weren't in the house.
I had the case down off the wardrobe.
It was not a bad decision and I'll not sit at this table and have anyone call it one." "So what changed it?" "I've told you.
He went down to look at the water." "That's not an answer, Avoa." Her grandmother looked at her then, properly, over the bowl.
"No," she agreed.
"It isn't." "And he came back up an hour later and he never mentioned Liverpool again." Maeve waited.
"That's the whole of it, love.
I've never had another word out of him about that evening and I've stopped asking.
Some things a person needs to keep whole."
